title: Formal conditional probability and independence
bigPicture: The conditional probability formula makes 'given that' precise and gives a numerical test for independence.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you use the formula for P(A | B)?
keyIdeas.answer: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), so P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) × P(B). From a table: divide the joint count by the total of the given row or column.
A and B are independent if P(A | B) = P(A) (equivalently P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)). Calculate both sides, compare and state a conclusion.

keyTerms.def: probability of A given that B has happened
restricts the sample space to B

workedExamples.title: From a table
workedExamples.prompt: In a class, 12 of 20 girls and 6 of 10 boys walk to school. Find P(walk | girl) and decide whether walking is independent of gender.

misconceptions.right: Generally not; divide by the probability of the GIVEN event.
That is P(A ∩ B) for independent events only.

practice.prompt: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.4. Find P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∪ B), and determine whether A and B are independent.

Year 12: 45 play sport, 35 do not. Year 13: 30 play sport, 40 do not. A student is chosen at random. Find P(sport | Year 12) and P(Year 13 | no sport), and test whether playing sport is independent of year.

assessmentNote: AA SL external exams: Paper 1 without a calculator and Paper 2 with a GDC, both written answers in sections A (short) and B (extended); no multiple choice. Practice prompts here are original and are not predictions of exam questions.
